A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Zero-AVSR work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary MARC statistics are readable and support a complete comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction tests, MuAViC recognition results, ablations, noise experiments and Japanese Common Voice results for the proposed systems.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds unseen-language noise experiments and qualitative failure examples.

M1.justification: The AV-Romanizer, cascaded pipeline, unified Zero-AVSR architecture, CTC objective and two-task LLM adaptation remain unchanged. The suggested incorporation of prosody is future work.

E1.justification: Section 5.4 extends evaluation to noisy zero-shot recognition of unseen Spanish and Russian; v1's noise experiment covered seen languages. The datasets, language inventory and Japanese out-of-domain evaluation remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 1–7 retain the same comparators, including AV-HuBERT, u-HuBERT, both XLAVS-R sizes, MMS Zero-shot and the tested LLM variants. The added noise experiment uses the existing audio-only versus audio-visual comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds individual-language CER measurements across -5 to 15 dB SNR for unseen Spanish and Russian alongside the existing nine-language WER experiment. Section 5.6 also describes feeding ground-truth romanization into the LLM to isolate de-romanization errors. Previously reported training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds targeted unseen-language noise robustness tests and a qualitative analysis separating romanizer errors from LLM de-romanization errors, illustrated by four examples. The existing dataset-size, LLM, language-family and Japanese analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new figures retain point-result reporting without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing table values and Japanese CERs of 60.9% for Cascaded Zero-AVSR and 64.9% for Zero-AVSR are unchanged. V2 adds Figure 4's CER curves showing greater visual benefit under stronger noise and Figure 6's failure examples; these are additional results, not improved scores for the retained experiments.

T1.justification: The speech-feature definitions, fusion equation and zero-shot assumptions are unchanged. No mathematical derivations, theoretical results or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and concluding summary retain the claims concerning the two zero-shot AVSR frameworks, language-agnostic representations and the 2,916-hour, 82-language MARC corpus.

C2.justification: Section 5.6 attributes most errors to romanization and identifies improving the AV-Romanizer as a priority. The new Limitation paragraph explicitly discusses weak LLM support for low-resource languages and loss of tone, stress and vowel-length information, extending v1's existing discussion of LLM dependence and non-reversible romanization.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies that romanization uses unaccented Roman characters, providing a limited representation detail without establishing a procedure change. The implementation settings, MARC construction instructions and code/model access links otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 65 cited works and related-work positioning are retained. Bibliographic differences concern pagination and citation back-references, without new research comparisons or novelty claims.

P1.justification: V2 expands Section 5.4 and adds Section 5.6, a Limitation paragraph and Acknowledgments. These are localized insertions; the earlier narrative and section organization are largely preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds a noise plot as Figure 4 and error examples as Figure 6. V1's Japanese examples move to the following page and become Figure 5. Existing figures and tables otherwise retain their designs, with subsequent content reflowing.

improvement.justification: V2 directly supports noise robustness in unseen languages and explains failure modes and applicability limits more clearly, while preserving the original evidence. The gains are bounded: the new noise test covers two languages, and the assertion that most errors arise in romanization has no reported counts.
